title: Bands, clubs, Kid Thomas, Mamaloos camps, fish fries and lawn parties
summary: Miller lists the bands and clubs he worked in, how Stackolee taught him piano, the Last Round-Up, Kid Thomas, Kid Clayton at Mamaloos and the lake camps, and begins describing fish fries and lawn parties.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Can you remember some of the other bands you've worked with? You told about that first band that you played, the one on Dryad Street. I worked with Paul Barber, I worked with George Lewis, I worked with George Williams, I worked with the average band around here. Yeah, I guess you worked with a whole bunch of them. Yeah, around here. Like most of the musicians. I worked with Kit Howard, Sheik, Thomas, you know I work with Thomas now. I work with Thomas now. But I worked with Peter Burkhardt, I worked with Willie Humphrey, Pryce Humphrey, I worked with all of those guys. I've been playing with all of them since I was a kid. Almost all of them. But they all knew I could play. There's a lot of musicians that say they can play, but they can't play. That's true. Still there's a lot of good musicians here too. Yes. People that I've never heard of. My uncle, you may have known him, Eddie Johnson. Eddie Johnson, the bass player. Oh, the bass player. He was the only bass player besides Tillman and Brown. I knew a few bass players. He plays tuba. He plays tuba. Is he much older than you? My uncle? Oh yes, he's older than my dad. Older than your dad? Yeah. Sometimes, you know, his uncle's just a few years older than a person. Yeah, he's older than my dad. In fact, him and my dad was in the same band. In other words, they used to play for the Jolly Boys and Girls, the Young Men Olympia, and the Mary go around, and the Buzzs and all those people like that. Did you ever play in any brass band, any instrument in the brass band? I never played in a brass band. First day she bought a piano. She bought a piano from the league. She paid ten dollars for the piano. And soon I'd come in from school every evening, I was on the piano. She could call me to watch this show, I was still on the piano. Yeah. Trying to not have to play. I used to take my two fingers and go along the keyboard and listen. Yeah. Other words, I had control of this right hand and never to have control of the left hand. So one day, I heard a guy playing, and I listened to what he was doing on the piano, and from then on I was playing. From playing. Who was it, do you know, that you listened to him? Ian Brose? That was Stackel E. It was Stackel E. Yeah, it was Stackel E. See Stackel E, he said, there were about two doors of me. We lived on Sixth Street then. He's dead now, isn't he? No, he's working back at Millen Home, right now. He is? Where? At Millen Home. He works there? Yes. Back there on St. Bernard. The one down on Franklin and all that? That's right. No, the one on St. Bernard. St. Bernard. Back there on Cadillac Street. Yeah, I don't know of that. Does he still play piano? No, he doesn't play any more. I didn't think so. I mean, I used to hear about him all ten or fifteen years ago a little bit, but then I never, I don't remember if I heard him or not. I might have, on Bourbon Street someplace once, I'm not sure. No. What style did he play? Mostly blues? Well, he was more of a hollong piano player. A what? A hollong piano player, you know. Like the hollong? He was a blues piano, but he was more of a blues man, you know. In other words, he couldn't play too many sentimental numbers. Never could play too many sentimental numbers. But I listened to whatever he did, I tried to learn it myself, but that's what started helping me out, started to learn the keyboard. Now when I first started, I played F sharp. Well, in the black keys. In the black keys. Yeah. A lot of guys I learned to do that. Then, I worked with a group a couple of times, they couldn't even tune up at the piano, and I had a cross chord. In other words, I played E natural, B natural. Yeah. That's the keys I played. And I didn't think I could do it. Well, one mind kept telling me, he said, once you can try to learn the different sounds. So I run the chromatic and then adjust some keys up and down, and see that heavy note in place, you see. Yeah. And that's the main line playing B natural. Many fellows can't play no B natural, E natural, F sharp. They can't play those kind of keys. They can't play D flat. Usually it's a hard key, I can say. Yeah. Somebody can read music, right? Yeah. Bothersome. I was going to ask about some of the different clubs and the old halls, dance halls that you played in, if you can remember. Well, I worked at the Bulls. I worked at the Tulane Club back down on Gravity Street. Yeah, I know. Which bands did you play with then, or did you work by yourself sometimes? No, I never had worked by myself. Up until lately, I do work by myself now. I worked by the gas light on Sunday night by myself. You know, over there. Yeah. But I have worked a gang of jobs by myself. In fact, I worked a job, I didn't want no band, just wanted to play a piano player. And I'm going to play these work jobs myself. Were there any of the other old time dance halls, like, well, the old Economy Hall or Quadraters Hall? Well, I worked at the last round up. I worked at the Lulule. I worked at the Lulule, right down here. Yeah. And this was sent to you down here. I worked at those different clubs. Other way, I worked the last round up. That was the last place closed up down here. That was the last jacket closed up down here, called the last round up. It would be open, the other jacket would be closed. I used to go right down there at night, from seven o'clock at night, and be down there at five, sixty o'clock the next morning. And music was what you call a real deal there. A dollar and a half was plenty money for musicians at that time. A dollar and a half. Depression days, huh? Yes. But I made a dollar and a half. In other words, my tip was more than my salary was. Yeah. My salary was a down and a half. My tip would be about twelve, thirteen o'clock. A night. That wasn't bad then. Yeah. That was every night. But I actually started off playing music out, like I told you, with those guys, Julius Simpson, Eddie Hickman, and Cliff Bruce. Cliff Bruce. I didn't put his name in there, but that's his name, Cliff Bruce. Cliff Bruce. That's his name, Cliff Bruce. And we started there. Yeah. When did you first play with Kid Thomas? After Joe James died. No, he hired Smitty before he got me. But him and Smitty couldn't even get out when I was nice. You had never played with Kid Thomas before in the old days? I had played with Kid Thomas when Kid Thomas was playing across the river at the... What's the name of the place over there? That place is Moulin Rouge. Moulin Rouge. Is that it? Yes. Now, Kid Thomas was playing at Moulin Rouge, and I was working down at Seymour's Coconut Grove. I worked there five years with Earl Foster. In other words, Kid Thomas had his band. He still had the same piano player, and we had four pieces, and Kid Thomas had about six pieces down by the moon. But after we'd knock off, I would go down there sometime, and listen to Kid Thomas play. And sometimes I would sit in with the band. That's during that time. That was around 1940. I'd sit around 46, 46. I remember sitting there on Dad's Dune too. Dad's Dune too. Dad's Dune was a piano player. He used to try to show me how to play piano, but I was much better piano player than him. He was. So instead of him showing me, I used to show him. But he was supposed to be showing me. So he liked it in my style. That's Dune. He was leader of a band then, was he? Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Do you remember who else was in his band at that time? Well, we had a banjo player called Emmet. Emmet. He used to drink too much. I didn't take him away from that drink. I used to tell him all the time, he wouldn't be drinking too much. Did you ever play out at the Millenburg, out the lake there in those camps? I was playing at the Millenburg. I used to play at Mamaloos. Oh, yes. I played at Mamaloos. I used to play at Mamaloos. Yes, I played at Mamaloos. I played at Mamaloos with Kid Clayton. Oh, yes. I knew him. I played out there with Kid Clayton. When he used to go out there and renovate him for fifteen cents. And catch the Smokey Mary train going back there. Plenty of people don't know about the Smokey Mary. I remember the Smokey Mary. Yeah. I remember the Smokey Mary. I used to go back there or catch the Cemetery Court and ride straight on back west end to the end of the line. Where did you play at west end? West end, yes. Did you play at any of the places out there? Camps? That's the Mamaloos. Mamaloos was right on the lake. The camp. That's where I played. Right on the water. I played out there about three years with Kid Clayton. Then I was playing the Badger there. Oh, you played Badger there. I played Badger there. I played Badger there. I played music with Jerry Green, bass player. I played, I come up under Papa John, bass player down there. Slow drag. I don't remember him playing no bass but I remember him being a Grand Martian. I never even knew he could play no bass. I think he was mostly a dancer and he played a little guitar and the homemade bass he finally made himself. Yes. But Punch, you see Punch downstairs, Punch used to coat one of my aintes. I have to make him remember that the name. Punch Miller, he used to coat one of my aintes. Yeah. But he's no relation to your family at first. No, he's no relation to my family at all. He may be related to my daddy, my daddy in the Chamberlain in the Barlet. Yeah. Just like I have an uncle named Eugene Miller. Well, it was a long time before I knew he was my uncle. In other words, I played with Joe Harris, he's a scientist one player too. Yes, I remember he lived up on... Chapitou Street. Chapitou Street. Is he still living there? No, that's my first cousin. Is that right? That's my first cousin to my daddy's people. In other words, Joe Harris was kin to me on my grandfather's side. And I played with him about six years and didn't know it. My first cousin. Didn't know he was my cousin. Yeah, we interviewed him about four or five years ago. Yes. He had some nice pictures of some of the early bands he played in. I don't suppose you have any pictures of any of those early bands that you played in? Oh, no. I had a gang of pictures from Littlewoods. I'm with my second wife now and then my first wife at the road staff. Yeah. So I didn't keep up with too much. Yeah, most people lose those pictures. They don't bother to keep them. Yeah, I didn't keep up with them. They're interesting to look at now. I do have some pictures of Earl Foster at home now. Yeah. With Austin Young and Mr. Willie James and myself. That was the four. That was the band. That was during the time I played at the Coakland Grove across the river. Was Austin playing the trombone there? No, he was playing the bass. Playing the bass. Playing the bass. I took some pictures of him playing bass. I made records of him with some of the bands. It reels almost over, but can you remember anything else about the camps out at the lake and the bands you heard there, what went on out there? Was it mostly private parties or were they clubs open to the public or how? No, these were private parties that we played for out there. Private parties. Yes. These were private parties that we played for out there. When the time I played with Fifth League. Oh. Can you tell us more about the lawn parties? The lawn parties? That you went to and played for and all? Well, most of my lawn parties was at those fraternities up on, uptown. Yeah. Those were the most lawn parties I played. None down here. No. Yeah. And this was sent to down here. And the fish fries when you were a boy? Yeah, fish fries when I was a boy. They had a red light, you say, out there on the street? Red light on the street. On the gate. Yes. Did they charge to get in or did you just go in and buy your fish or what? Just go in and buy your fish. You go in and buy your fish and come out. Some people would stay and listen to the music. Would they have a band or just the piano player usually? The piano player, sometimes a guy would have a guitar and somebody would come out there with a harmonica. Yeah. Red light on the street. We'd start in the evening around at 6 o'clock and round up around 5 o'clock the next morning. Well, they'd go all night then. They'd go all night until the fish was out. That's during my time. Were they mostly right in the house or did they have it out on the lawn? Well, some of them have it in the yard. They'd have tables in all the yard. Yeah. Sit in the yard. You'd be sitting at a table sit in the yard. In other words, during that time people would look for houses with big backyards there to give these poils and fish fries and things. Did anybody just have them or did certain people have them almost every week? Oh, they had fish fries. Some nights they had fish fries two in one block. That often? Just that often. They'd say, well, we go to Miss Elizabeth's house or someone else's house. We go to our fish fries. Or we go to our Miss Phyllis's fish fries. She'd go to the night. They'd always have music though, would they? Oh, they'd always have music. And doing that, if they didn't have music, they had to wind up graffinals, you know, with those big .
